q: Do I need a Chinese company to sell to Chinese customers?
a: Not always. You can export to China through a local importer, sell cross-border through a platform, or license a product to a Chinese company without ever registering an entity. You need an entity when you must issue a Chinese fapiao, employ staff locally, hold a sector licence, receive RMB from domestic customers, or open a local bank account. Start with the job the entity has to do — see [Do you need a China entity at all?](/guides/do-you-need-a-china-entity/).

q: Can I own and run the company from abroad?
a: You can own a Chinese company without living in China, but running it remotely is harder than it looks. The legal representative signs documents and is personally accountable; the bank requires a face-to-face account opening; tax and labour filings need a local representative. Many absentee owners appoint a Chinese legal representative and a local finance manager, which works until the two disagree.

q: Can I just use a Chinese friend's company to invoice?
a: It is common, cheap, and one of the most expensive mistakes available. You have no ownership, no control of the bank account, no claim on the revenue, and you are relying on the friend's tax compliance. If the relationship ends, the customers, the contracts and the money stay with the company. Nominee arrangements exist but need a written trust and a lawyer, not a favour.

q: What can a foreigner not do in China?
a: Foreign nationals cannot register as individual businesses (个体户) or sole proprietorships, so the smallest legal vehicle is a company. Beyond that, the negative list prohibits or restricts foreign investment in a specific set of sectors — news and publishing, film production, compulsory education, and parts of telecoms and finance among them. The licence regime can be stricter than the ownership rules.

q: WFOE, joint venture or representative office — which one?
a: A WFOE if you want to trade, invoice and control the company; a joint venture if the sector requires a Chinese partner or you need their licences and relationships; a representative office only if you need a liaison presence and will never invoice from China. Most founders who think they need a JV actually need a WFOE and a local distributor — [the comparison](/guides/wfoe-jv-roe-comparison/) sets out the trade-offs.

q: Can I own 100% of a Chinese company?
a: Yes, in any sector not on the negative list. Since the 2024 edition of the list, manufacturing is fully open and most service sectors allow wholly foreign-owned companies. The constraint is usually the sector licence, not the ownership rule: a WFOE can be 100% foreign-owned and still be unable to operate a clinic, a school or a payment business without a licence it cannot get.

q: Do I need a Hong Kong holding company?
a: No, not as a legal requirement. A Hong Kong company can hold the mainland WFOE, which helps with future offshore financing, currency and a possible exit, and it may access a better treaty rate on dividends. It also adds an audit, a registered office, annual filings and a layer of ownership that Chinese banks will ask about. A holding company with no substance is decoration, not structure.

q: How much registered capital should I put on the licence?
a: Enough to fund the business through its first year and to satisfy any sector licence minimum, and no more. Registered capital is a promise that must be paid within five years under the 2023 Company Law, and shareholders are liable up to it. A large number looks credible until the deadline arrives; a number too small can fail a licence threshold or a bank review.

q: Can I add a Chinese shareholder later?
a: Yes, by transferring equity, which requires a shareholder resolution, an amended articles of association, tax clearance on the transfer and a registration change. It is easier than starting over, but the valuation and the tax on the transfer are negotiated at that point, when you have less leverage than you did at incorporation.

q: What does it actually cost to set up?
a: For a straightforward service WFOE in a tier-one city, budget roughly ¥20,000–¥60,000 for the first year including the registered address, agency fees, seals, bank account and bookkeeping. Add the sector licence, a fit-out, an EIA or a factory lease and the number moves by an order of magnitude. The [setup-cost tool](/tools/setup-cost/) breaks the lines out.

q: How does money get into the company?
a: Three legitimate routes: equity (registered capital into the capital account), a shareholder loan (registered with the bank and foreign-exchange authority), and revenue from customers. Each has different tax and repatriation consequences. Wiring money to the legal representative's personal account is not one of the routes, however common it is.

q: How do I take profits out of China?
a: Dividends are paid after corporate income tax and after making up losses and statutory reserves, with 10% withholding tax unless a treaty reduces it. Service fees and royalties can be paid to a foreign affiliate if they are genuine, documented and priced at arm's length. Salary is the simplest route and the most heavily taxed. The [repatriation tool](/tools/repatriation/) models the dividend case.

q: Do I need a Chinese bank account?
a: Yes, for any operating company. Salaries, taxes, social insurance, rent and customer receipts all run through the corporate account, and the fapiao system is linked to it. Opening the account is a face-to-face process that can take longer than the registration itself — see [Opening a corporate bank account](/guides/opening-a-corporate-bank-account/).

q: What taxes will the company pay?
a: VAT on sales (13%, 9% or 6% depending on the activity, with a 1% rate for small-scale taxpayers through 2027), corporate income tax at 25% — or an effective 5% for qualifying small low-profit companies — plus stamp duty, surcharges and payroll taxes. The rates are national; the enforcement and the local incentives are not.

q: Can I employ myself as the foreign founder?
a: Yes, and in most cases you should. The company signs an employment contract with you, pays a salary, withholds individual income tax and social insurance, and sponsors your work permit. A founder who takes no salary creates a work-permit renewal problem and a thin tax record that banks and licence reviewers notice.

q: Do foreign employees need a work permit?
a: Yes. Every foreign employee needs a work permit tied to that employer, graded A, B or C. Category B, which covers most founders and professionals, requires a bachelor's degree or higher, two years of relevant experience and a salary above the local threshold. The employer must be registered, taxed and able to show the payroll.

q: What does an employee really cost?
a: Take the gross salary and add employer social insurance and housing fund contributions, which commonly run 25–40% of salary depending on the city and the contribution base, plus severance accrual and recruitment cost. A ¥20,000 monthly salary is closer to ¥27,000–¥28,000 in cost before any bonus.

q: Can I fire someone?
a: Yes, but not at will. China requires a statutory ground — performance after documented improvement, misconduct, redundancy with consultation — and severance of one month's salary per year of service, or two months for an unlawful dismissal. Probation dismissals still need a documented reason. This is the clause founders most often get wrong in the contract.

q: What has to be filed every year?
a: The market-regulator annual report between 1 January and 30 June; the corporate income tax settlement by 31 May; the foreign-exchange annual declaration for companies with foreign capital; monthly or quarterly VAT and payroll filings; and an annual audit for most foreign-invested companies. The [compliance calendar](/guides/annual-compliance-calendar/) lists them by month.

q: What happens if I ignore the filings?
a: The company goes on the abnormal-operations list, which blocks bank account changes, bidding and sometimes invoicing. Fines accrue, the legal representative's name is attached to the record, and closing the company later becomes slower and more expensive. The registrar's system is connected to the bank's, so it is not a private matter.

q: How do I close a Chinese company?
a: Liquidation first — creditors, employees, tax, assets — then tax clearance, then deregistration of the business licence, then the bank accounts and seals. A clean company with no disputes takes six to twelve months; a company with unpaid tax or a departed shareholder takes longer. [Closing a company](/guides/closing-a-company-in-china/) walks through the sequence.

q: Can I just abandon the company and leave?
a: The company does not disappear. It keeps accruing filings and penalties, the legal representative can be restricted from leaving China or from serving as a legal representative elsewhere, and the foreign shareholder's record is affected. Abandonment is the most expensive way to close a company.

q: How long does the whole setup take?
a: For a service WFOE with no sector licence, four to eight weeks is realistic: name self-declaration in a day, registration in one to two weeks, seals in a week, the bank account in two to four weeks and tax onboarding in another week. A licenced business — food, education, healthcare, finance — adds months, and the licence, not the registration, sets the date. [The compliance calendar](/guides/annual-compliance-calendar/) covers what comes after.

q: Who should be the legal representative?
a: Someone who is a director or manager and actually executes company affairs — that is the legal requirement under the 2023 Company Law, not a formality. The role carries personal exposure: consumption restrictions, the dishonest-debtor list, and limits on leaving or serving elsewhere if the company fails. A foreigner can hold it, but needs a work and residence permit tied to the company. Read [the legal representative guide](/guides/legal-representative-and-seals/) before agreeing to hold the role for someone else.

q: Do I need to register a trademark?
a: If the brand matters, yes — China is first-to-file, so whoever registers first owns it, including a distributor or a former employee. File the Latin name, the Chinese name and the logo as separate marks in the classes you trade in. The official fee is around ¥300 per class electronically, and the process takes nine to twelve months, which is why filing early is cheaper than opposing later.

q: Can I change the company name or scope later?
a: Yes, by a change registration (变更登记), usually one to two weeks with a new licence and updated bank and tax records. The name goes through the same self-declaration and conflict check; the scope change may trigger a licence review if you add a licensed activity. Changes after a licence is granted are also a common moment for a bank review, so keep the file consistent.

q: Can I use a virtual address?
a: Only if it is a real, staffed address that the registry, the bank and the tax bureau can each verify. Addresses sold for registration only are the most common cause of an abnormal-operations listing, which freezes banking and invoicing. Co-working and serviced offices sell legitimate registration addresses; a PO box or a borrowed flat does not.

q: Do I have to issue a fapiao for every sale?
a: Yes, if the customer is a company that needs to deduct the cost, and in practice for most domestic revenue. Small-scale taxpayers can issue at 1% through 2027; general taxpayers issue 13%, 9% or 6% depending on the activity. The invoice must match the contract, the payment and the declared revenue — mismatches between the three are what tax audits look for.

q: Can I import goods and sell them in China?
a: Yes, but the company needs customs declarant registration, and the product may need pre-market registration — GACC registration for food, NMPA for cosmetics and some devices. Import cost is tariff plus import VAT (13% for most goods, 9% for some) plus consumption tax on categories such as alcohol, tobacco, cosmetics and vehicles. Only a general taxpayer can credit the import VAT, which is often the reason to give up the small-scale status.

q: How long does closing the company take?
a: A simplified deregistration with no debts can finish in one to two months; a full liquidation with tax clearance usually takes three to six months, and longer if there are unpaid taxes, departed shareholders or staff disputes. The creditor notice and announcement periods cannot be shortened. A company that has kept its filings closes fastest.

q: Do I need a visa before I register the company?
a: No. A company can be registered with an apostilled passport and shareholder documents, and the legal representative can sign through an agent or at a consulate. What needs a visa is working in China: the company must exist before it can apply for your work permit notification, which is the basis for the [Z visa](/guides/business-visa-and-entry/) and then the residence permit.

q: Can I run the company on a 30-day visa-free entry?
a: No. Visa-free entry and a tourist visa cover meetings, inspections and signing, not employment. Working on them is unauthorised employment, with fines and possible deportation for you and penalties for the company that benefited. Convert to a Z visa and residence permit before you start operating from China.

q: Do I have to take a Chinese partner?
a: Only if the activity sits on the restricted list of the foreign-investment negative list, or if a sector regulator requires local ownership. The national list still has 29 items, with 27 in the free trade zones. Most manufacturing, trading, consulting, software and design activities need no Chinese shareholder, and a [wholly foreign-owned company](/guides/wfoe-jv-roe-comparison/) is simpler to control.

q: My overseas company serves Chinese clients — does China tax it?
a: It depends on permanent establishment, not on where the contract is signed. A fixed place, a service project longer than the treaty threshold (often 183 days in 12 months), a construction site or a dependent agent in China creates a PE, and the attributable profit is subject to 25% corporate income tax plus VAT. Short visits and genuinely independent distributors usually do not. See [the PE guide](/guides/tax-residency-and-permanent-establishment/).

q: Can I pay a management fee to my overseas parent?
a: Yes, but the Chinese company withholds 6% VAT and 10% corporate income tax on the payment, unless a treaty reduces the rate and the beneficial-owner conditions are met. The fee also has to be arm's length and supported by a real service. Many structures are simpler with a dividend than with a management fee.

q: Is an annual audit mandatory?
a: For a foreign-invested company, in practice yes. A licensed Chinese CPA firm audits the annual accounts, and the report is needed for profit distribution, for the bank when dividends are remitted, and often by the tax bureau. Budget ¥5,000–20,000 and appoint the firm before the end of April. See [bookkeeping and the audit](/guides/annual-audit-and-bookkeeping/).

q: Does my website need a Chinese company behind it?
a: If it is hosted in mainland China, yes: an ICP filing is issued to a Chinese legal entity that owns the domain, and the site is filed through the hosting provider. A foreign-owned company can hold the filing, but some content categories need an ICP licence instead, which is closed to foreign control. Hosting outside China avoids the filing and costs speed. See [ICP filing and hosting](/guides/icp-filing-and-hosting-in-china/).

q: Can my company hire another foreigner?
a: Yes, once the company itself is registered and has a tax and social-insurance record. The employee needs a work permit — usually Category B, which requires a bachelor's degree plus two years of relevant experience — an apostilled criminal record check and a medical exam. Budget one to three months and 1.2–1.5 times gross salary in total cost. See [hiring foreign employees](/guides/hiring-foreign-employees/).

q: Do I need a Chinese privacy notice and consent flow?
a: If you handle personal data of people in China, yes. PIPL requires a lawful basis, a Chinese-language notice, separate consent for sensitive data and for minors under 14, and one of three mechanisms before any data leaves the country. Small exports are exempt under the 2024 thresholds, but the limits are annual and cumulative. See [personal data and PIPL](/guides/data-compliance-pipl/).

q: Can I advertise my product as the best in China?
a: No. The Advertising Law bans absolute claims such as 最佳, 最高级 and 国家级, and platforms remove listings for using them. Some categories — medicines, medical devices, medical services, health food — need a pre-approval certificate before any ad runs. False advertising fines start at three times the ad spend with a ¥200,000 floor. See [advertising rules](/guides/advertising-and-content-rules/).

q: Can a foreigner open a school or a clinic in China?
a: Not freely. Compulsory education is closed to foreign investment and academic-subject tutoring is effectively closed to foreign capital; preschool, high school and higher education only through Sino-foreign cooperative schools with Chinese control. Medical institutions are JV-only outside a 2024 pilot allowing wholly foreign-owned hospitals in nine provinces and cities. See [education access](/guides/education-and-training-access/) and [healthcare and devices](/guides/healthcare-and-medical-devices/).
